title: Carlsen and Nakamura: what the numbers show
outcomes: Quotes a measured habit together with its sample size and period
Names at least one thing a given number does not show
States what extra data would be needed before drawing a conclusion about a player

steps.text: This lesson compares **Magnus Carlsen** and **Hikaru Nakamura** on a few things we can count. It does **not** say who plays better, who is bolder, or what kind of player either one is. Every number comes from our own archive of games where both players were rated 2400 or more, with duplicates removed. Counts and percentages are computed from that file (built 2026-10-29).

steps.prompt: Before the numbers: what is one thing you would want to know about a player's games before saying anything about their style?

steps.text: **Sample.** Carlsen: 5,654 games in our data, 2012 to 2026. Nakamura: 7,612 games in our data, 2012 to 2026. These are the games our archives hold, not everything either player played. Average game length: Carlsen 47.2 moves, Nakamura 48.9 moves. Average opponent rating: Carlsen 2685, Nakamura 2658. Source: docs/player-stats.json.

steps.prompt: Before reading the results, write a guess: which player's draw share in our data is higher, and by how much? Then see whether the next card agrees.

steps.text: **Results.** Draws as a share of all games: Carlsen 1,671 of 5,654 (29.6%), Nakamura 2,226 of 7,612 (29.2%). With White, Carlsen won 1,769 of 2,869 (61.7%); Nakamura won 2,329 of 3,946 (59.0%). With Black, Carlsen won 1,368 of 2,785 (49.1%); Nakamura won 1,806 of 3,666 (49.3%). Both samples are in our data, 2012 to 2026.

steps.prompt: Look at the results card. The draw shares are 29.6% and 29.2%. What does that small gap NOT show? What would you need to check before saying either player draws more?

steps.text: **Queens and openings.** Games that reached move 30 with queens still on: Carlsen 2,716 of 4,948 (54.9%), Nakamura 4,062 of 6,635 (61.2%). First move with White: Carlsen played e4 in 1,234 of 2,869 games (43.0%) and Nakamura in 1,209 of 3,946 (30.6%); Nakamura played Nf3 in 1,234 of 3,946 (31.3%), Carlsen in 277 (9.7%). These are choices in our data, and opponents and preparation shape them.

steps.prompt: Look at the queens-and-openings numbers. Name one reason, other than the player's taste, that could make a game reach move 30 with queens on.

steps.text: **Limits.** We did not count each game's format or opponents; our file only says the games are standard-rate games from two sources (The Week in Chess issues and Lichess broadcasts from 2020). The two players may have faced different opponents and tournaments. Our data holds some of each player's games, so a different archive could give different shares. Queens on at move 30 says nothing about why. Do not turn any number into an adjective.

steps.prompt: Pick one number from the cards, such as the 54.9% against 61.2% of games with queens on at move 30. Write what it does NOT show, and one more thing you would need to check (for example, game format, opponents, or years) before using it to describe how either player plays.

steps.text: **How to read such claims.** Ask four questions. How many games? Which years and which opponents? What exactly was counted? Could the choice have been forced by the situation? A claim with a sample size and a stated measure can be checked; a claim like 'he plays X chess' cannot. For further reading on checking sources, see the Library page in this app.

steps.prompt: Write one sentence about either player that uses a number, the sample size and the years, and makes no claim about style. Then write what a stronger claim would need.

sources: docs/player-stats.json (built by tools/player_stats.py from the local game archives, both players rated 2400+, de-duplicated)
